slides.title: Ultrasound changes the flight of unrestrained moths
body: Free-flying moths exposed to artificial **ultrasound**, sound above the human audible range, changed course or stopped beating their wings. Roeder photographed these responses on an open lawn rather than restricting the insects to a wire or tether.

A marker flash identified stimulus onset, and interruptions in the photographic tracks provided a 0.25-s time base. Flash-only trials caused no flight deviation; enclosing the camera reduced unwanted ultrasound from its shutter.

Some moths made passive dives with motionless wings, whereas others continued powered flight. Recorded reaction times ranged from 0.2 s to more than 1 s. These field observations establish ultrasound-evoked flight changes, but bright illumination and incomplete species identification limit conclusions about natural darkness and species-specific responses.

slides.title: Weaker ultrasound elicits flight away from the source
body: At greater distances from the source, or after the ultrasonic output was reduced, moths turned and flew away from the loudspeaker. This **directional avoidance** changed the flight path relative to the source, rather than simply reducing altitude.

The source position was fixed while naturally flying moths crossed the illuminated area. Moths approaching the source could reverse their course; those below it sometimes descended, and those above it could turn upward.

Turning away occurred whether the resulting path carried an insect toward, away from, or across the light gradient. The comparison supports an acoustic contribution to direction. It does not identify the central comparator that converts differences between the two ears into asymmetric wing movements.

slides.title: Stronger stimulation recruits varied diving maneuvers
body: Moths closer to the transducer exhibited a range of escape maneuvers: sharp passive dives, powered dives, loops, tight turns, and climbs followed by descents. Their common tendency was movement toward the ground, rather than a uniform direction away from the source.

Roeder usually repeated ultrasonic pulses 30 times per second. The stimulus continued while flight was photographed, allowing the trajectory after sound onset to be distinguished from the insect’s preceding movement.

Wing movements could cease or increase in frequency after stimulation. The behavioral distinction between weaker-source avoidance and stronger-source diving is supported by these records. A simple assignment of each maneuver to one receptor cell is not established, because the experiment did not selectively manipulate auditory neurons or reliably identify every responding species.

slides.title: Three-dimensional tracking measures actual bat attacks
body: Corcoran and Conner recorded long-legged myotis bats, _Myotis volans_, pursuing naturally flying moths in an outdoor enclosure. Infrared cameras registered predator and prey positions without the visible floodlighting required by Roeder’s photographic method.

The enclosure measured 6 m by 4 m, with a height of 2.2–3 m. Synchronized camera views were calibrated and reconstructed into three-dimensional trajectories, linking movements in space to the outcome of each encounter.

A turn observed from one camera can conceal changes in altitude or depth. Reconstructed trajectories resolve those components and permit measurements of speed and turning performance. The encounters reveal real pursuit and evasion, but the enclosure and available moth assemblage constrain generalization to every hunting habitat and predator species.

slides.title: Evasion greatly reduces capture during aerial pursuit
body: In the observed bat–moth encounters, bats captured 37.5% of evasive prey but 98% of non-evasive prey. Evasion was identified by sharp turns or accelerations during the attack, rather than by labeling every surviving moth as evasive.

Infrared video linked each movement sequence to capture or escape. Non-evasive moths followed comparatively slow or broad paths, whereas evasive moths changed speed or direction abruptly as the bat approached.

The comparison connects flight behavior with survival in this preparation. It does not prove that every difference arose from hearing alone: moth species, body form and flight performance also differed. Successful evasion therefore requires analysis of the actual maneuver as well as the sensory signal that may have initiated it.

slides.title: Noctuid ears connect the tympanum to sensory neurons
body: A **tympanum** is a thin membrane that vibrates in response to airborne sound. In noctuid moths it occupies a recessed region of the posterior thorax, near the junction between thorax and abdomen.

Roeder and Treat described a sensory attachment on the membrane’s inner surface, enclosed within the tympanic air sac. The **tympanic nerve**, a bundle carrying sensory axons, runs from this apparatus toward the thoracic ganglion.

This anatomy provides a mechanical route from external sound to sensory tissue and a neural route into the central nervous system. The published anatomical reconstruction identifies named supporting structures, but it is not a measurement of vibration or a complete synaptic map. Its functional interpretation depends on the separate nerve-recording experiments.

slides.title: Sensory attachments couple membrane motion to the ear
body: The noctuid tympanic sensory organ contains two **scolopes**, specialized supporting elements associated with sensory-cell dendrites. A dendrite is the peripheral region of a sensory neuron that receives the mechanical stimulus, whereas its axon carries the resulting signal centrally.

The sensory attachment extends inward from the tympanic membrane and is supported by a ligament and surrounding tissues. Roeder and Treat’s published section represents these relationships while explicitly leaving some cellular details presumptive.

Two acoustic response units were subsequently distinguished in the nerve recordings. Agreement between anatomy and physiology supports a small receptor population, but the section does not identify a mechanically gated ion channel or prove the exact force experienced by each dendrite. Those molecular and mechanical questions require different measurements.

slides.title: Sound recruits acoustic units within the tympanic nerve
body: An **afferent** is a neuron carrying information from a sensory organ toward the central nervous system. Roeder and Treat recorded afferent spikes extracellularly from the tympanic nerve after separating it from central connections.

An extracellular electrode detects voltage changes produced by nearby action potentials, the brief electrical impulses propagated along axons. Sound produced rapid trains in two acoustic units; a larger, regularly recurring non-acoustic unit remained insensitive to the stimulus.

The non-acoustic discharge commonly occurred at 5–20 spikes per second. Separating this activity from sound-evoked spikes prevents every nerve event from being counted as hearing. Different acoustic thresholds distinguish receptor units even when their recorded spike sizes overlap; recording amplitude alone is an unreliable cell label.

slides.title: Vibrometry links membrane motion to neural activity
body: **Laser Doppler vibrometry** measures surface motion from changes in reflected laser light. In _Noctua pronuba_, ter Hofstede and colleagues directed the laser at the tympanum’s sensory-cell attachment while presenting calibrated sound pulses.

The method recorded velocity, the speed of membrane motion, and displacement, its excursion from the resting position. Stimuli lasted 20 ms and sampled frequencies from 5 to 80 kHz; incident sound was measured beside the ear.

Simultaneous auditory-nerve recordings linked mechanical responses to spike production. Measuring the same attachment rather than an arbitrary membrane location constrains the relevant receptor input. These observations describe the physical stimulus to the sensory cells, but they do not identify the molecular channel that first converts force into membrane current.

slides.title: Displacement predicts the threshold for auditory spikes
body: A **neural threshold** is the lowest stimulus satisfying a stated response criterion. Across 15–80 kHz, the tympanic displacement at threshold remained approximately constant, whereas the corresponding membrane velocity increased with frequency.

The mean threshold displacement was 140 pm for A1 and 2510 pm for A2. A picometre is one trillionth of a metre. A1 and A2 denote the more sensitive and less sensitive acoustic receptor cells, respectively.

Sound-pressure thresholds alone combine the ear’s mechanical response with the receptor’s sensitivity. The stable displacement thresholds support displacement as the relevant mechanical input under these pure-tone conditions. They do not prove the identity or gating properties of a transduction channel, and the relationship differs at the lowest tested frequencies.

slides.title: Dissection preserves near-threshold membrane motion
body: Exposing the auditory nerve could alter the ear’s biomechanics. Ter Hofstede and colleagues therefore compared the same moth in intact flight orientation, intact inverted orientation, and an inverted preparation with the nerve-recording electrodes inserted.

Near neural threshold, tympanic velocity and displacement showed no consistent difference across those treatments. Sound levels were defined as **dB SPL**, a logarithmic sound-pressure measure referenced to 20 µPa.

At stronger stimulation, particularly below 35 kHz, dissected preparations could show greater membrane movement than intact animals. The control supports near-threshold recordings as estimates of intact hearing under the tested conditions. It does not validate every suprathreshold response or every frequency-modulated bat call, because those conditions were not equivalently tested.

slides.title: Sound-level meters can bias pulse-duration comparisons
body: A conventional sound-level meter can average brief pulses through its time-weighting circuit. For the published 1.5–50-ms pulses, holding the displayed reading constant can require different true pulse amplitudes when duration changes.

Thevenon and Pfuhl reanalyzed published moth recordings using a mathematical account of meter damping. Their article compares original duration-dependent spike curves with curves after the assumed measurement bias was corrected.

Corrected pressures change the apparent relation between duration and spike count. This retrospective reanalysis supplies no new moth recordings. Missing meter settings prevent complete reconstruction of the stimuli, so its correction depends on assumptions rather than direct historical calibration.

slides.title: Repetition-rate effects depend on amplitude calibration
body: Thevenon and Pfuhl also examined published spike responses to pulses repeated at 20, 33, 50 or 100 Hz. More frequent pulses occupy more of the meter’s averaging interval, so a matched displayed level need not mean matched instantaneous sound pressure.

Their published correction aligned much of the repetition-rate dependence in the reanalyzed dataset. The result raises a calibration-based alternative to interpreting every reduction in spikes per pulse as neural adaptation.

The analysis depends on the modeled damping circuit and information reported in the original methods. It does not establish that adaptation is absent in all moths or all stimulus sequences. A stronger test measures the local sound waveform directly and compares responses under a clearly defined amplitude convention.

slides.title: Wax-moth membranes respond across a broad bandwidth
body: The greater wax moth, _Galleria mellonella_, has four auditory receptor cells per ear, contrasting with the two-cell noctuid system. Moir and colleagues measured membrane movement optically to determine how broadly its tympanum responds to ultrasound.

At 90 dB SPL, membrane oscillations exceeded 1 nm throughout the tested 50–300-kHz range. A nanometre is one billionth of a metre. Maximum movement occurred at the sensory attachment, rather than uniformly across the membrane.

A mechanically responsive tympanum does not establish neural hearing at every tested frequency. The membrane must move enough to activate its receptors, and neural responses were measured separately. The broad mechanical bandwidth is an observed property; its proposed advantage for rapid temporal responses remains an interpretation requiring behavioral tests.

slides.title: Wax-moth receptors respond at frequencies up to 300 kHz
body: Moir and colleagues recorded the wax moth’s auditory nerve during 20-ms pure-tone pulses. A response criterion requiring repeated sound-associated spikes reduced the chance of mistaking spontaneous firing for an auditory response.

The lowest measured threshold was approximately 55 dB SPL at 80 kHz. In responding animals, thresholds rose to approximately 83 dB SPL at 280 kHz and 87 dB SPL at 300 kHz; some animals did not respond at the maximum tested 90 dB SPL.

These recordings establish neural sensitivity to exceptionally high frequencies in this preparation. They do not establish effective flight avoidance at 300 kHz or a natural bat threat using that frequency. The ecological purpose of the extended sensitivity was unresolved in the study.

slides.title: Constant displacement stabilizes A1 response latency
body: **First-spike latency** is the delay between stimulus arrival and the first auditory action potential. Ter Hofstede and colleagues measured A1 latency while holding either membrane velocity or displacement constant across frequencies.

At constant displacement, the first spike remained near 7 ms over most of the tested range. At constant velocity, latency increased with frequency. The relationship was consistent with the displacement-based thresholds obtained independently.

Displacement constrains receptor excitation more closely than velocity under these conditions. The experiment links the mechanical input to the timing of neuronal output, rather than only to the presence of spikes. The extracellular record still does not separate the receptor’s generator potential from the subsequent ionic mechanisms producing an action potential.

slides.title: A1 and A2 sample different sound-level ranges
body: Gordon and ter Hofstede compared acoustic thresholds in noctuid and erebid moths using extracellular auditory-nerve recordings. An **audiogram** is the relationship between stimulus frequency and the level needed to evoke a specified response.

The moths were most sensitive between 15 and 55 kHz. A2 thresholds generally exceeded A1 thresholds by 15–20 dB. At 5–10 kHz, substantially stronger sound was needed, and thresholds also increased at higher ultrasonic frequencies.

The two cells expand the range of sound levels that can influence the nerve signal. Threshold separation does not assign a distinct behavior to either neuron. It also does not imply that the animal discriminates pitch, because frequency-dependent sensitivity can exist without an output that uniquely identifies sound frequency.

slides.title: A2 extends coding after A1 activity begins to saturate
body: **Range fractionation** divides a sensory intensity range among receptors with different thresholds. In moths, A1 begins responding at lower levels and A2 is recruited when the sound is stronger.

Gordon and ter Hofstede measured separate A1 and A2 spike counts for 50-kHz pulses lasting 2, 5, 10 or 20 ms. Longer pulses often permitted A1 output to increase toward the level at which A2 began firing.

For short pulses, A1 could reach a plateau before A2 was recruited, leaving a gap in count-based intensity coding. slides.title: A sustained tone rapidly adapts the acoustic response
body: **Adaptation** is a reduction in sensory response during continuing or repeated stimulation. Roeder and Treat followed the more sensitive acoustic unit during a sustained 70-kHz tone and counted its spikes over time.

In that recording, the initial rate approached 1000 spikes per second, fell to about half that rate within 0.1 s, and reached roughly one quarter by 1 s. A slower decline continued toward an irregular discharge near 90 spikes per second.

The result establishes a time-dependent change in the peripheral output despite continuing sound. It does not identify whether the change originates in receptor mechanics, transduction or spike-generating conductances. Because sound pressure was not measured in this particular experiment, the curve cannot be assigned a precise absolute intensity.

slides.title: Stronger pulses shorten peripheral response latency
body: Roeder recorded tympanic responses to repeated short ultrasonic pulses while increasing amplitude in calibrated increments relative to an individual preparation’s threshold. This isolates changes in timing and spike count from changes in pulse frequency or duration.

After subtracting the 2.9-ms sound-transmission delay over 1 m, the biological response time ranged from approximately 3.2–4.0 ms near threshold to 1.9 ms at the strongest tested level. Timing was also more variable near threshold.

The shorter delay is consistent with faster excitation of the receptor as sound grows stronger. The generator potential was not successfully measured intracellularly, so its rate of rise remained an explanation rather than an observed mechanism. An external onset marker permits this latency measurement; a flying moth must obtain useful timing information from its own sensory signals.

slides.title: Total spike count does not predict pulse effectiveness
body: Roeder compared free-flight behavior during pulsed ultrasound and continuous tones of the same frequency and amplitude. Turning away occurred much more often with pulses, while tones elicited more total A1 spikes during a matched recording interval.

For the 60-kHz comparison, 3-ms pulses repeated 30 times per second were compared with a continuous tone. Recordings made at different source distances linked the same acoustic conditions to the nerve response.

Tones produced longer spike trains but adapted more rapidly; pulses repeatedly generated short-interval bursts. The result rejects total afferent spike count alone as a sufficient explanation of behavioral effectiveness. It supports sensitivity to temporal organization, without proving the exact central filter that selects the effective pattern.

slides.title: Thoracic repeaters relay the afferent burst
body: An **interneuron** is a central neuron connecting sensory input with other central processing or motor pathways. Roeder recorded sound-responsive activity within the thoracic ganglia, the central nerve-cell clusters associated with flight control.

Some units closely repeated the A1 burst but fired later. These **repeater neurons** included crossed responses passing to the opposite side and ipsilateral responses continuing toward the head. Simultaneously recorded A1 and repeater spikes differed in their temporal ordering.

The recordings establish central transmission of tympanic input and some transformation during longer stimuli. They do not establish a complete sequence of identified synapses. A synapse is a functional junction between neurons; the extracellular observations did not identify its transmitter, receptor subtype or postsynaptic ion channels.

slides.title: Bilateral summation differs from a direction comparator
body: Some recorded units responded to stimulation of either ear, and simultaneous stimulation produced a larger discharge. **Bilateral summation** combines input from the two sides rather than necessarily comparing which side received the stronger signal.

Roeder presented matched 5-ms ultrasonic pulses to the right ear, the left ear or both. A summating unit near the ganglion midline could produce a bilateral response resembling that evoked by stronger stimulation of one ear alone.

Such activity establishes convergence of auditory inputs but is insufficient by itself to identify a directional difference detector. Steering requires a relationship between side-specific information and motor output. The proposed subtraction or temporal-precedence mechanisms were not directly resolved by this recorded summating response.

slides.title: Pulse-marker units transform bursts into single events
body: A **pulse-marker neuron** usually generated one spike after an A1 burst, even when the burst contained several spikes. This transformation reduces the detailed duration information in the afferent train while retaining the occurrence of an acoustic event.

slides.title: Pulse-marker recovery depends on the afferent pattern
body: The pulse-marker response depended on a preceding interval with reduced afferent activity. A long continuous A1 train often generated only one central spike, even when short interspike intervals continued after the initial response.

Averaged responses could appear smoothly graded, but individual moths retained A1 saturation ranges of 4–12 dB before A2 recruitment. body: A moth can hear a bat that is attacking another insect. Corcoran and colleagues defined a **real threat** as an attack on the focal moth and a **false threat** as an attack on a neighboring free-flying moth.

Synchronized infrared video and ultrasonic recordings estimated call pressure at the focal moth while reconstructing bat position. During real attacks, received intensity generally increased before leveling late in the approach. During false threats, intensity at the non-target moth tended to decrease.

slides.title: Field clicking begins during early-to-middle approach
body: Corcoran and colleagues recorded free-flying bats passing tethered _Bertholdia trigona_ and compared encounters that elicited clicks with those that did not. The focal moths could hear and click, but their flight trajectories were constrained.

Clicking usually began during early-to-middle approach, with bat pulse intervals of 25–60 ms. Sound level at the moth discriminated clicking from silent passes more consistently than bat distance or flight approach angle alone.

These observations link natural acoustic input with the onset of a defensive output. They do not establish that tethered and freely flying moths respond identically, or that a fixed distance determines clicking. Timing depends on what the insect receives acoustically, including whether the bat directs its calls toward it.

slides.title: Rising call levels precede defensive clicking
body: During the interval preceding defensive clicks, bat calls increased in received intensity while their pulse intervals became slightly shorter. Corcoran and colleagues measured these changes over the 250 ms before clicking onset.

The acoustic combination is consistent with a bat detecting and targeting the moth. In real attacks, received intensity could subsequently plateau near 95 dB peSPL while the bat reduced its source output as it approached.

A decreasing emitted level therefore need not mean decreasing threat at the prey. Geometry and source regulation jointly shape the signal that reaches the ear. slides.title: Escape does not require greater speed than the bat
body: Corcoran and Conner compared maximum flight performance during measured bat–moth encounters. Bats exceeded evasive moths in speed and several acceleration measures, yet many evasive moths escaped.

The bats’ advantage also included tighter minimum turn radii and greater peak turning performance. Non-evasive prey generally performed worse than evasive prey, but comparing maximum values alone did not determine the outcome of a chase.

A moth can exploit the timing and geometry of a maneuver rather than outrunning the bat along the same path. The comparison concerns the recorded movements within this predator and prey assemblage. It does not establish a universal performance ranking for all bats and moths.

slides.title: Turning performance combines speed and turn radius
body: **Radial acceleration** describes the change in velocity direction during a curved turn. A tighter turn at a given speed requires greater radial acceleration; speed alone omits the geometry of the motion.

Corcoran and Conner extracted turn speed, radius and radial acceleration from reconstructed flight paths. Moth radial acceleration increased with turn speed, whereas bat radial acceleration was much less dependent on turn speed in the measured range.

These differences constrain the maneuvers available during pursuit. They do not imply that a moth must exceed the bat’s maximum acceleration to survive. The relevant outcome depends on whether a particular turn changes the interception path before the bat can follow it, rather than on one isolated performance value.

slides.title: Sharp turns and smaller escape angles favor survival
body: The **escape angle** is the direction of the moth’s movement relative to the approaching predator. Corcoran and Conner measured it after the initial evasive turn, along with the moth’s radial acceleration.

Moths escaping with angles of 40–100° survived more often than those taking angles above 100°. Escaping prey averaged an angle near 83°, whereas captured prey averaged near 126°. Greater radial acceleration also distinguished successful maneuvers.

Turning partly toward or across the approaching bat can therefore be more effective than continuing directly away during a chase. These are measured associations within the tested encounters, not a command that every moth should follow one fixed angle. The sensory and motor mechanisms choosing the trajectory were not identified.

body: _Bertholdia trigona_ produces dense ultrasonic clicking in response to attacking bats. Its tymbal has a specialized surface associated with sound production, documented by scanning electron microscopy.

The clicks occupy time and frequency ranges capable of interfering with returning echoes. **Sonar jamming** means disruption of the bat’s use of echoes for prey localization, rather than simply making the moth audible. body: Corcoran and colleagues presented tethered moths to trained big brown bats in a flight room while recording attacks with infrared video and ultrasound. Silent palatable moths provided a comparison with clicking _Bertholdia trigona_.

slides.title: Persistent protection supports jamming over startle
body: A startle defense should weaken as a predator becomes accustomed to the sound, whereas a learned warning should change as the predator associates the signal with an unpleasant prey item. These alternatives predict different attack patterns over repeated experience.

In Corcoran and colleagues’ experiment, protection from _Bertholdia trigona_ clicks appeared immediately and persisted over successive nights. Bats that ate the moths still had difficulty contacting clicking individuals, and attacks often continued after the sound began.

The pattern supports sonar interference over a purely transient startle effect or learned rejection of distasteful prey. Individual bats differed in palatability responses, so the strongest interpretation concerns those that consumed the moths. The experiment supports jamming without identifying one exclusive neural mechanism of echo disruption.
